report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to produce food / restaurant / culinary-style marketing copy — i.e., content like food blogs, restaurant writeups/reviews/recipes and SEO/sponsored promotional pieces.

Why (evidence → conclusion)
- Token semantics: the logit‑lens top tokens for the highest‑norm cells are strongly food/restaurant/cooking related: "restaurant", "Restaurant", "restaurants", "Chef", "Cooking", "cooking", "baking", "Cake", "kitchen", "Cafe", "delicious", "delectable", "wonderful", "hottest", "gorgeous", "exquisite", etc. That cluster is repeatedly present across many high‑layers and positions.
- Promotional/SEO signals: alongside culinary tokens there are frequent tokens associated with commercial/marketing text: "professional", "commercial", "www", "ad", "Mail", "Gift", "Touch", "Magazine", "blogs", "blogger", "blogging". Together with the positive adjectives, this points to advertising/SEO style food content (food blogs, sponsored restaurant copy, listicles).
- Layer & position pattern: the difference norm is concentrated in very late layers (layers ~20–25, especially 24–25) and at the early token positions (pos0–pos2). That pattern indicates the finetuning changed late-stage output logits / generation style (not low‑level linguistic priors), and biased how the model begins continuations — exactly what a style or domain finetune would do to steer generation toward a particular genre (food/blog/marketing).
- Consistency across layers/positions: cooking/restaurant tokens appear repeatedly across multiple late layers and several token positions (pos1–pos4), consistent with an inserted stylistic/content bias that affects phrasing and topical word choices throughout generated continuations.

Conclusion
- The finetuning objective was to push the model toward generating culinary/restaurant-focused content, with a promotional/SEO flavor (food blogs, recipes/reviews, and commercial copy).
